task: Check Java parity on the positive Phase 20 FileIO runtime integration fixture.
observation: The C++ checker accepted the fixture while Java rejected RangeBatch indexing and iteration. After adding those checked types, both checkers accept it, but generated Java Rust contains only length-based __MossFile/__MossRange placeholders; C++ emits the production moss_fileio and moss_root_runtime implementations with actual file operations.
impact: Checker parity for the exercised source shape was incomplete, and passing --check still does not imply usable native FileIO: Java codegen drops the open mode and lacks writes and batch reads. This is a backend implementation gap beyond the intentional Fast Debug FileIO limitation.

resolution.summary: The Java checker now accepts the RangeBatch fixture. Java codegen now bundles the production FileIO and root runtime, lowers checked read/write/sync/close calls, translates FileIO errors, and lowers bounded inline batch requests, RangeBatch indexing/iteration, and Range byte iteration. Java unit tests pass. Native compilation/execution and executor Solo-hook integration remain unverified.

task: Validate Java checker and generated Rust for the accepted Phase 20 FileIO request-record-vector form.
observation: The checker had accepted inline FileIO batch literals but rejected a named finite request vector, even though the native generator needed that form to lower the request records into offset/size pairs. The checker now retains a bounded-vector proof for literal request records with literal finite sizes, invalidates it on mutation, aliasing, or a call that receives the vector, and rejects unbounded vector parameters. Generated Rust lowers the surviving named vector through read_batch_checked. A follow-up read-before-batch probe found the proof invalidator was treating indexed reads as writes; invalidation now applies only to indexed assignment targets, and the read-before-batch positive case passes.
impact: Checker acceptance and native lowering had mismatched profiles for a documented batch-read shape. The bounded proof now closes the named local-vector case while refusing unknown or mutated request sets.

resolution.summary: Java ABI-v9 and staged ABI-v10 suites pass all 12 test classes. Positive named-vector codegen/checker coverage includes a read before batch use; unbounded parameter and mutated vector cases reject with FILEIO_UNBOUNDED_REQUEST. The proof remains a bounded local subset; full FileIO flow parity and native validation remain outstanding.

task: Wire FileIO Solo blocking notifications into Java Executor scheduling.
observation: The production FileIO root runtime had a configurable Solo hook table, but Java Executor supplied neither worker-aware callbacks nor process-root registration. FileIO blocking on an Executor worker could therefore occupy a worker without triggering compensation. Java codegen now registers worker-aware callbacks in FileIO-enabled mains, and the Executor tracks Solo nesting, starts a bounded compensating worker when runnable capacity falls below the configured base, and retires excess workers when they become idle again.
impact: The old generated combination implemented real FileIO and Executor independently but did not connect their blocking behavior. That left Executor progress guarantees incomplete for FileIO workloads.

resolution.summary: ABI-v9 and staged ABI-v10 Java tests pass; generation assertions cover hook registration and bounded worker logic. The standalone JAR and launcher also generated the FileIO fixture with runtime resources and callbacks present. No generated Rust compile or native runtime execution occurred; worker behavior remains unverified pending the frozen-candidate gate.

task: Compare FileIO typed-error handling at the process root between C++ and Java.
observation: C++ rejected a `main` that allowed FileIO errors to escape and a `recover FileError.IO` arm that left other open/read variants unhandled. Java accepted both. Java now treats FileIO operations as raising all six FileError variants at root validation, follows those variants through helper calls, and subtracts variants caught inside the helper; focused probes show the same accept/reject outcomes as C++.
impact: The Java checker could accept programs whose generated native error path had no root handler, even though the C++ compiler rejected them. The gap affected both direct operations and helper propagation.

resolution.summary: Focused C++ and Java probes now both reject unhandled direct FileIO errors and partial FileIO recovery. Java ABI-v9 and staged ABI-v10 suites pass all 12 classes, including a helper that handles FileIO errors internally. Native error-carrier compilation and execution remain outstanding.

task: Compare root-local FileIO close analysis across Java and C++.
observation: With all FileIO errors handled, C++ still rejected a root that left an opened file unclosed and a root that closed only on one branch; Java accepted both. Java now tracks root-local open/close state through if/else, try/recover, and zero-or-more loop joins. Focused probes match C++ for unclosed, partially closed, and both-branches-closed cases. A follow-up exposed that Java also accepted a read after close and a read after a branch left lifecycle state uncertain. The root flow now rejects those as FILEIO_CLOSED_OPERATION and FILEIO_UNKNOWN_STATE. Open-mode tracking now distinguishes read-only handles; a write after `FileIO.open(path, ro)` previously passed in Java but now produces the same FILEIO_READ_ONLY error as C++.
impact: FileIO resources require explicit close on every normal exit. The previous Java checker could accept leaking roots and could not distinguish a complete branch close from a partial close.

resolution.summary: C++ and Java agree on root close/lifecycle probes, after-close and uncertain-state operation diagnostics, and read-only write rejection. All-branches-close is accepted. ABI-v9 and staged ABI-v10 suites pass all 12 classes. Helper-managed owners, domain fields, and complete lifecycle parity remain unfinished.
